PART 1 — WHO WE ARE: Spirit, Soul, I-Am-Nots, and Belief Formation

1.1 New Creation and Ongoing Renewal (resolving the "spirit man" question)

Two sentences are both true and sit at the base of everything that follows: "You are a new creation; your spirit is alive and your identity is settled" (2 Cor 5:17; Eph 2:5), and "You are being renewed in mind, healed in heart, and formed in body and relationship" (Rom 12:2; 2 Cor 4:16; Ps 147:3). Scripture's grammar is indicative ("you are...") followed by imperative ("so put off, put on, be renewed..."). The imperative does not cancel the indicative; it is how the new identity gets lived out. "Heart" and "mind" overlap throughout Scripture (Eph 4:23 says "the spirit of your mind"; Eph 1:18 prays for "the eyes of your heart") — so a sharp claim that believers are "only spirit" and need no heart care sits uneasily beside Psalm 147:3, Isaiah 61, Hebrews 12:15, and Peter's own heart-level restoration in John 21. The illustration that holds both: a child adopted at six is a full son the day the papers are signed — nothing more is needed for sonship — yet he may still flinch at raised voices for years. Parents don't say "you have no wounds, just think correctly," nor "you are your wounds." They say "you are ours" and stay close while he learns to live at home. Everything in Parts 2 onward is that staying-close work, built on a foundation that was never in question.

Where they agree: the mechanism (belief, not the event, is the cause), the inner pain, the self built around it, and where healing happens (Jesus's I AM met inside the I-am-nots). Where Kruger adds something: an upstream distorted-God-picture layer, and five named coping methods. Where emphasis differs: the sermons stress disidentifying ("that is not me"); Kruger stresses being met within the I-am-nots and learning to live from Jesus's I AM from inside them — the observer stance is a first step, not the whole of healing.

1.4 The Defender and the Seeker Across the Five Methods

1 Self-salvationPrimary — ambition, credentials, winning, staying on topPrimary — earning love: usefulness, perfectionism, over-serving
2 NumbingSecondary — work, control, drink, entertainment when the cover cracksSecondary — food, screens, romance, sleep, withdrawal, substances

Both postures lean hardest on methods 1 and 5 — which is why pride and longing look so different on the outside and so similar underneath: both are asking people for a verdict the Father has already given.

Being valued, and wanting to be valued, are not wrong. The trouble starts when identity rests on it — guarding it (Defender) or chasing it (Seeker). Both place the answer in people's verdicts instead of the Father's.

1.5 Does Everyone Have I-Am-Nots?

Short answer: nearly everyone, though not equally — in Kruger's framework the natural mind's distorted God-picture sits under every soul, no environment is perfect, the tempter's whisper targets identity itself (Matt 3:17/4:3 — right after "this is my beloved Son" comes "if you are the Son of God..."), and because I-am-nots form by belief, they can come from small repeated messages, not only big wounds.

QUIETACTIVEACUTE
Rarely triggered; mostly secure; still holds some false picture of God or selfRegular triggers and covers; relationships and peace affectedTrauma, abuse, crippling anxiety, depression or addiction
Ongoing discovery of unionGuided heart-healing, community, the practices in Part 4 (of the uploaded series)Spiritual care plus professional help; safety first

Some people are genuinely secure with few intense triggers — secure attachment and resilience are real. For them there may be little to "heal," though the journey of discovery and a rebuilt vision of God continues lifelong. No one is beyond needing the gospel; not everyone needs intensive heart-healing.

A caution: use this on yourself first; it is not a diagnostic tool for others. Quiet I-am-nots in a person doing well should not be treated as hidden wounds, and the absence of obvious symptoms does not mean there is nothing left to discover in Christ.

1.6 How Beliefs Actually Form (Connecting to Childhood Development)

Kruger's diagram says I-am-nots enter "by faith, by belief" — but belief does not arrive from nowhere. The earlier study in this series, Belief Formation & Character Development, traced exactly how: experiences are interpreted (usually by caregivers) into core beliefs, which crystallize into self-concept, which generates automatic thoughts, which drive repeated behavior, which over years becomes character. That pipeline is the mechanism by which an I-am-not gets "believed" in Kruger's sense.

This is why Part 1.5 above is true: belief, not trauma alone, is the channel. A thousand small comparisons in school-age years can plant "I am not good enough" just as effectively as one large wound — which is also why self-esteem (Section 1.7) and character (built from 10,000 hours of repeated small choices, as the Belief Formation study details) end up so tightly bound to the I-am-not framework.
